To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in patients with coronary artery disease who undergo coronary angiography, the site of acute MI can be predicted on basis of a previous angiogram.

in a selected medically treated cohort of patients, acute myocardial infarc-tion is frequently related to segments that were not the most stenosic one or were not even significantly stenosic at previous angiography and that this is particularly true with a long interval (more than 2 years) between the first angiography and acute myocardial infaction.
in a selected cohort, AMI frequently occurs in a segment that was previously not significantly stenotic or not the most stentosed segment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms of myocardial infarct and with the development of a non-invasive technique for the early detection of myocardial infraction.
the development and evaluation of a new, non-invasive, non-radioactive method for measuring myocardial blood flow.
the development of a method to detect and quantify the degree of stenosis in a coronary artery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the site of an AMI is not predictable by the most severe coronary stenosis at the previous coronary angiogram.
the most severely stenosed coronary artery segment on the first angiography is a poor predictor of the site of future AMI.
in a selected cohort of medically treated patients, the site of AMI is not predictable from the site of the most stenosed coronary artery at a previous angiography.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the severity of coronary artery disease on angiography does not necessarily predict the future site of myocardial infarctions, and that the site of myocardial ischemia and infarction is frequently related to the site of a new coronary stenosis.
the site of myocardial infarct is not related to the site of most severe stenosis on previous coronary angiography.
the site of AMI is often not related to the most severe stenosis at previous angiography.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the site of acute MI cannot be predicted on the sole basis of a previous angiogram, and that the severity of the narrowing is a poor predictor of future AMI.
the site of an infarct may be unrelated to the most stenosed segment at the previous coronary angiogram.
the most significant stenosis on the angiogram may not be the culprit lesion in an acute myocardial infartion.
